title: He Put the Man in the Garden — Rest, Garden, Bone
blocks: Brothers and sisters, last time we read Genesis chapter 1. That chapter kept the camera very far back — from chaos to the heavens, from light to humanity, six days walked through, and God says "very good." Today the camera suddenly comes in close. The same God, the same event, but this time the author brings the camera down to ground level, crouches, and lets us watch him work clay in his hands, watch him plant a garden with his own hands, watch him bend down and set the man inside it.

And the question this chapter puts to us is thoroughly practical: do you also feel that you have to produce something before your life counts? Once the studies are finished, the job is secure, the house is bought, the children are on track — then you are entitled to draw breath.

Let me give you the answer up front: the man was made on the sixth day, and the seventh day is rest. So the first full day a human being ever lived was not a day of striving; it was a day of resting with God. You do not work your way into rest. You are placed in rest first, and that is where the strength to work comes from.
1. The Seventh Day: the Only Stretch of Time That Was Blessed

Chapter 2 opens like this: "The heavens, the earth, and all their vast array were finished. On the seventh day God finished his work which he had done; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done."

The word "rested" is וַיִּשְׁבֹּת (*vayishbot*), which literally means "he stopped." It shares a root with "Sabbath", שַׁבָּת (*shabbat*). Brothers and sisters, notice that this word does not mean "recuperate" or "get his strength back." Isaiah 40:28 says plainly that God does not faint and is not weary. So the seventh day is not God being tired; it is the work being finished, so that he can stop and enjoy it.

Then verse 3 says two things that happen here for the first time in the Bible: God "blessed the seventh day, and made it holy." This is the first appearance of the word "holy", וַיְקַדֵּשׁ (*vayqadesh*), which means "set apart." And look carefully: the first thing God ever set apart as holy is not a place, not a mountain, not a person — it is a stretch of time.

Brothers and sisters, this matters enormously for our age. What we find hardest to set apart for God is usually not money; it is time. The house can be given, but not Saturday morning. The money can be laid down, but not the calendar. Yet the first thing God declares holy in all of Scripture is time.

And one more detail: each of the first six days closes with "there was evening and there was morning" — only the seventh does not. The author left a gap. Hebrews 4:9 explains that gap: "There remains therefore a Sabbath rest for the people of God." That day has not ended, so you may enter it today.
If God never grows tired, what does it actually mean that he "rested" on the seventh day?

"Rested" (שָׁבַת) means to stop, not to recover strength. Isaiah 40 says it plainly: "he doesn't faint. He isn't weary." So the seventh day is not God needing a break; it is God laying down a pattern for us. And notice that the seventh day is the only one with no "there was evening and there was morning" — in the text it stands open, waiting for people to enter it. Hebrews 4 picks that up exactly: "There remains therefore a Sabbath rest for the people of God." So what rest really means is stopping your own work in order to enter the work God has already finished. Whether you are willing to stop today is not a question of stamina; it is a question of faith. Do you believe this world will keep turning for one day without you?
Keeping the Sabbath was Old Testament law. Do New Testament Christians still need to keep it?

The New Testament does not make the keeping of a particular day a condition of salvation — Colossians 2:16 says, "Let no one therefore judge you in eating or drinking, or with respect to a feast day or a new moon or a Sabbath day." But be careful not to read "do not let anyone judge you" as "you do not need rest." The principle of rest is older than the law; it stands there from Genesis 2, cut into the rhythm of creation itself, not first cut into the tablets at Sinai. So the healthy approach is not to argue about which day, but to face one honest question: is there any fixed stretch of my week in which I stop and hand sovereignty back to God? A person with no such stretch will eventually pay the bill in exhaustion, irritability, or his body. Freedom is not doing without rest; freedom is being able to stop holding everything up yourself.
2. Dust and Breath: Who You Are
Verse 7 is the most famous line in the chapter: "Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul."

Three words in that verse must be looked at. The first is "formed", וַיִּיצֶר (*vayyitser*). This is not the same word as "create" (בָּרָא) in chapter 1 — בָּרָא is bringing something out of nothing; וַיִּיצֶר is what a potter does with clay. In chapter 1 God speaks; in chapter 2 God works with his hands.

The second word is "dust", עָפָר (*afar*). This is the humblest material in a human being, and Genesis 3:19 — "you are dust, and to dust you shall return" — uses exactly the same word. And notice: "man" is אָדָם (*adam*) and "ground" is אֲדָמָה (*adamah*) — his origin is carried in his name. It is a very weighty Hebrew pun: your name is the place you came from.

The third word is "breathed", וַיִּפַּח (*vayipach*). This is the only time in the whole Old Testament that God is recorded breathing into a human being. And John 20:22 says that the risen Lord Jesus breathed on his disciples and said, "Receive the Holy Spirit!" Brothers and sisters, the same act, thousands of years apart, appearing a second time. The first made a living man; the second made a new man.

So what are you? You are half dust and half the breath of God. Both have to be remembered together. Remember only the dust and you will live without dignity; remember only the breath and you will live without proportion. Psalm 104:29 says, "You take away their breath; they die and return to the dust." Your breathing is on loan — and that one sentence is enough to bow the proudest head, and enough to lift the most defeated one.
If a human being is dust plus a breath, where exactly is the difference between us and the animals?

The difference is not in the material; it is in where that breath came from. Verse 7 says God "breathed into his nostrils the breath of life", and that word "breathed" (נָפַח) is an intimate act — you can only do it face to face. When the text describes the animals, that line is absent. Chapter 1 has already given us "in our image", which is identity; chapter 2 adds relationship: this is a creature God breathed into himself and set in place with his own hands. Put the two together and the meaning is this — human dignity does not rest on capability, it rests on having been personally drawn near to by God. So caring for someone who can do nothing at all is still caring for someone who carries the breath of God. And when a person lives as though he were only dust, that is not humility; it is forgetting who breathed into his nostrils.
3. Put, Cultivate, Keep — the Man Who Was Placed There
Verse 15: "Yahweh God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to cultivate and keep it." Three verbs in that verse, and every one of them is worth stopping over.

"Put" is וַיַּנִּחֵהוּ (*vayanichehu*), and its root is the word for rest. So the more accurate picture is: God set the man down, and settled him there. The man did not find his own way into Eden. He was carried in and set down.

"Cultivate" is לְעָבְדָהּ (*le'ovdah*), a word later used in Leviticus for the priests' service in the sanctuary. "Keep" is וּלְשָׁמְרָהּ (*uleshomrah*), a word later used in Numbers 3:8 for the Levites keeping charge of the tabernacle. Brothers and sisters, do you see it? Both of those verbs later become temple vocabulary. Eden is the first sanctuary on earth, and Adam is the first priest.

That single observation overturns two very common misunderstandings. First, work is not the result of sin. Work existed before the fall; it is part of the blessing. What is cursed in chapter 3 is the ground — the yield of work becomes hard — not work itself. Second, the line between sacred and secular does not run through what you do; it runs through whom you do it for. The cultivating and keeping you do in your office is described with the same word as what the Levites did in the tabernacle.

Then verses 16 and 17: "You may freely eat of every tree of the garden; but you shall not eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil." Notice the proportion: an entire garden is permitted, and one tree is not. God says "you may" before he says "you may not." Any handling of this passage that makes God sound stingy has the proportions exactly backwards.
"Cultivate and keep" sounds like plain work. So is work a curse or a blessing?

Work existed before the fall, so work in itself is a blessing. What chapter 3 adds is not work but "the sweat of your face" and "thorns and thistles" — that is, toil and frustration. The distinction is very practical: what you hate is often not the work itself but the futility inside the work. And the word "cultivate" (עָבַד) is later used of a priest's service in the sanctuary, as is "keep" (שָׁמַר). In other words, the garden is the earliest sanctuary and humanity's first profession was priesthood. Once that is restored, your work sits on a different set of coordinates: you are not doing it for your boss, you are keeping a patch of God's earth on his behalf. That patch might be thirty students, one machine, a service counter, or a household.
4. It Is Not Good for the Man to Be Alone — the First "Not Good" God Ever Said

Verse 18: "Yahweh God said, 'It is not good for the man to be alone.'" Brothers and sisters, stop here. In chapter 1 "good" appears seven times, and "very good" once. Up to this point the whole creation account has run good, good, good. The first "not good", לֹא־טוֹב (*lo-tov*), comes before any sin has been committed, and what it names is this: a person on his own.

So loneliness is not the result of sin. Loneliness is the first gap God himself pointed at. This matters enormously for pastoral care: when a brother says he is lonely, that is not a sign that he is insufficiently spiritual. He has run into the very thing God called not good.

God's answer is עֵזֶר כְּנֶגְדּוֹ (*ezer kenegdo*), "a helper comparable to him." Both of those words have been misread. "Helper", עֵזֶר, occurs twenty-one times in the Old Testament, and in sixteen of them the subject is God himself — Psalm 121:2 says, "My help comes from Yahweh, who made heaven and earth," using exactly this word. A word used of God cannot suddenly mean something second-rate when it is used of a woman.
And כְּנֶגְדּוֹ literally means "corresponding to him, standing opposite him" — face to face, matching, someone he can look in the eye. Not beneath him. Across from him.

Then God does something rather strange: he first brings the animals and the birds to the man to be named one by one. And the end of verse 20 says, "but for man there was not found a helper comparable to him." Brothers and sisters, God let him go through a long search, creature by creature, that came up empty. Why? Because some gaps have to be felt by a person himself before a gift will be received as a gift.

Finally verse 22 says God made a woman from the rib. The Hebrew behind "made" is וַיִּבֶן (*vayiven*) — not "formed" but "built", the word used for building a house or an altar. And the first thing the man says when he wakes is a poem: "This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh." In Hebrew, "bone of my bones" is kinship language. It means: this one is my own.
God says "it is not good for the man to be alone" — does that mean an unmarried person is incomplete?

No. The verse says it is not good to be *alone*; it does not say it is not good to be *unmarried*. God's answer is a helper comparable to him, and the Hebrew word עֵזֶר (helper) is most often used in Scripture of God himself — there is nothing second-rate about it. More decisive still: the Lord Jesus himself was unmarried, and so was Paul, and Scripture never says either of them was incomplete. So what this verse is really saying is that human beings were not made self-sufficient; we need one another. Single people need real relationships, and married people cannot expect a spouse alone to fill that "not good" either. This is one of the reasons the church exists: so that a person without a spouse is still not alone.
God made the woman from Adam's rib — does that mean women are of lower rank?

The text runs in exactly the opposite direction. If order of creation established superiority, then humanity, made last, would rank below the animals. And the word "rib" (צֵלָע) is elsewhere in Scripture usually translated "side" — it is the word used for the side panels of the tabernacle. There is an old saying worth repeating: she was not taken from his head, lest she rule over him; nor from his feet, lest he trample her; but from his side, that she might stand alongside him. And what Adam says in verse 23 is "bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh" — that is a declaration of equality, not of hierarchy. Chapter 1 had already said it earlier: "God created man in his own image … male and female he created them." The image was given to both together.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot

The first is preaching "helper" as a lower position. This is one of the most common misreadings in Chinese churches. We have just seen that the word is used of God sixteen times. To preach it as assistant, subordinate, second-in-command is to read the text backwards. The test is simple: when you finish that section, will the women in the room feel they are supporting cast?

The second is arguing male superiority from who was made first. Order of creation never equals rank in Scripture — by that logic the animals were made before humanity, so are the animals higher? "Bone of my bones, flesh of my flesh" speaks of equality and correspondence, not of tiers.

The third is preaching Eden as a place where nobody had to work. Verse 15 says plainly "to cultivate and keep it." Preaching work as the result of sin will make your congregation loathe their workplaces, and will teach them that the spiritual life happens only inside a church building.

The fourth is preaching the boundary as God being hard on people. Mention only the one tree that is forbidden and never the whole garden that is given, and you have turned overwhelming grace into a restriction. What God gave was an entire garden.

The fifth is using "the two shall become one flesh" as a weight on single people. That verse institutes marriage; it does not rule that unmarried people are incomplete. The Lord Jesus was single, Paul was single, and Scripture never says a piece was missing from either of them. A single brother or sister should walk out of this chapter blessed, not wounded.
If rest matters this much, and I am so busy caring for my family that I have no time of my own, does that count as disobedience?

Start by separating "rest" from "doing nothing." The heart of rest is handing sovereignty back to God, not handing responsibility to somebody else. A person caring for small children or a bedridden parent is in a situation that does not permit stopping all day, and that is not disobedience. But here is a sentence to hear honestly: if you cannot give even ten minutes, the problem is usually not time — it is that you believe, inside, that things fall apart without you. So the practical step is to ask for one small piece: ten minutes, one bus ride, the half hour after the children fall asleep — and in that small piece do nothing else but hand the matter over to God. And let other people help you; refusing to be helped is sometimes its own refusal to rest.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: our culture prizes endurance and hard grind, working until the last breath — isn't a Sabbath just laziness? Brothers and sisters, this has to be answered on two levels. On the first level, affirm it: diligence is good, and the whole book of Proverbs praises the diligent. But the second level must be said clearly — there is a kind of diligence in Chinese culture that is really fear wearing a costume. The reason stopping makes us uneasy is that inside we believe our worth equals our output. And the opening of Genesis 2 dismantles that equation: the man was made on the sixth day and rested on the seventh. He was blessed before he had produced anything at all. So rest is not a permit for laziness. Rest is a declaration: I am not the one keeping this world fed.

The second question: my elders keep pressing me to marry, saying that not marrying is unfilial, that it means I am incomplete — can verse 18 be used to push someone like that? My answer is unambiguous: no. Verse 18 says it is not good to be alone. It names the gap of loneliness, and in Scripture God fills that gap in more ways than marriage. Psalm 68:6 says, "God sets the lonely in families" — and "family" there is not limited to marriage. The church is God's answer for a great many people. So pastorally we must hold both sides: on one side, take loneliness seriously, because it is real and God himself called it not good; on the other, refuse to make marriage the only exit, because that is neither biblical nor kind — it pushes single brothers and sisters further into the very loneliness you were trying to address.
7. Living 321 Out — Placed First, Then Put to Work
Brothers and sisters, let us tie this lesson back into the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model — the God of this chapter is a God who crouches down: he works clay, he plants a garden, he sets the man in place with his own hands, he puts the man to sleep before he operates. This God is willing to bend. And in John 13 the Lord Jesus takes off his outer garment, ties a towel around himself, and kneels down to wash his disciples' feet — the same stooping. My example is very concrete: be willing to bend down and serve one person.

The Bible is my standard — this chapter gives us the first commandment, and that commandment is given to a man who has not yet sinned. Which is to say: boundaries do not exist to deal with bad people; boundaries belong to being a creature at all. A standard exists not because you have misbehaved, but because you are human.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — the breath in verse 7 is the source of life. In John 20:22 the risen Lord breathes again. The way you have spiritual life today is the same way Adam had physical life: not something you drew in by effort, but something he breathed in.

Let Jesus be King — the tree in verse 17 is a sign, and what the sign says is this: the authority to define good and evil belongs to God, not to me. So the most concrete form of letting Jesus be King is this: there is something I could easily do and would very much like to do, and because he says no, I do not do it. A life with no territory at all marked "because he said no" has not yet let him be King.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — notice the subject of every verb in this chapter: God formed, God planted, God put, God commanded, God said it was not good, God brought, God built. The man does two things in this chapter: he names, and he sings a poem. Even his partner is made while he is asleep. Who the glory belongs to is written plainly here.

Establish God's system — the first system God established was not an institution but a relationship: the two shall become one flesh. So establishing God's system begins with building a home. A person who is greatly gifted at church and unwilling to bend down at home is building on sand. 321 says "life first, then relationships, then ministry", and this chapter is its biblical foundation.

And here I want to say something honest about 321 itself. We put great weight on selflessness, and rightly so — but this chapter reminds us that selflessness is not the same as having no boundaries. God's very first gift to Adam included a boundary. A person who, in the name of selflessness, never dares to say no and hauls everything onto his own shoulders is usually not humble; he is afraid. Real selflessness hands sovereignty to God — and the person who has handed sovereignty to God is precisely the one who dares to say no when God's word says no.
"Placed first, then put to work" — my current workplace is dreadful. Does that mean I have not been placed in the right spot?

Not necessarily. Adam was placed in Eden; Joseph was placed in Potiphar's house and then in a prison — and the text says "Yahweh was with Joseph" more often in the jail than in the house. So "being placed" is about who put you there, not about how comfortable there is. Two practical questions sort it out. First: is this place forcing me into sin or violating my conscience? If so, consider leaving, and leave properly. Second: if not, is there a patch here I can cultivate and keep? Do that patch well first. Many people begin by asking "is this my place?", but the order in the text is to do well the patch in front of you and let God move you to the next position.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One Sentence: "Not Good"
Brothers and sisters, the same chapter of Scripture, fed into different hearts, grows completely different things.

There is the proud heart. He finishes this chapter most confident of one thing — "I now understand the order of marriage" — and goes home to lecture his spouse out of chapter 2. Brothers and sisters, in this entire chapter the man says exactly one thing, and it is a poem of wonder, not a set of regulations. If the strongest impulse you feel after reading a chapter of Scripture is to correct somebody else, you have probably missed most of it.

There is the fearful heart. He does not dare stop, because the moment he stops the anxiety starts. A calendar packed solid is really a defence against the sentence inside that says "you are not enough." What God says to that heart is the seventh day: he stopped first. If the Creator stopped, your stopping will not bring the world down.

There is the ashamed heart. He feels he is nothing but a handful of dust — poorly educated, in poor health, from an ordinary family, nothing worth mentioning. Brothers and sisters, this chapter never denies that you are dust. It only adds one line: that breath was breathed by God himself. What is precious in you did not come built in — but it is real.

And there is the wounded heart. He may have been pressed down with the word "helper", told to submit, to endure, not to ask questions; or he may have been cut by something said from a pulpit about being single. Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: that word is most often used in Scripture of God himself. What wounded you was not this verse; it was somebody reading it backwards. And when God said "it is not good to be alone", he was standing on your side.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do

First, schedule a stretch of time that produces absolutely nothing. It does not have to be a whole day; start with two hours. No professional reading, no working through the to-do list — only Scripture, prayer, a walk. Deliberately go and experience it once: I stopped, and the world did not fall down.

Second, write down the one thing you are least willing to let go of, then ask yourself honestly: is this responsibility, or is this anxiety? Write the answer down and talk it through once with a spiritual companion.

Third, draw one boundary around one thing. A cut-off time, an event you will no longer attend, a topic you will no longer discuss. God's first gift to Adam had a boundary in it; draw yourself one this week.

Fourth, find someone you have never let close, and tell him one thing you are struggling with. God said it is not good to be alone, and the first step out of loneliness is not finding company — it is letting someone know.

Fifth, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church this week, in three sentences: the Bible says humanity was made on the sixth day and rested on the seventh, so the first full day a person ever lived was spent resting with God; which means a person's worth is not bought with output; and the first thing God ever called "not good" was a person being alone — so if you feel lonely, there is nothing wrong with you. God thought so too.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that my worth is not my output, and that I may stop, because God stopped first.
I declare that my breath is on loan, so I will not be proud; and that the breath was breathed by God himself, so I will not despise myself.
I declare that I will live freely inside the boundaries he has drawn, because that line is grace and not obstruction.
I declare that I will build the home before the ministry: life first, then relationships, and only then service.
Brothers and sisters, if only one picture from this lesson may remain, let it be the action of verse 15: he put the man in the garden.

Picture it. A lump of clay shaped into a man, who has not yet done anything, has not yet borne any fruit, has not yet proved whether he is worth it. And God bends down, lifts him up, and sets him inside a garden he planted himself — a garden whose name means "delight", for that is what עֵדֶן (*Eden*) means.
And the root of that word "put" is rest.

Brothers and sisters, this is the order of the gospel. You are not accepted after you work; you are accepted first, and then you work. Ephesians 2:10 says we are God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus "for good works" — created first, good works after, never the other way round.

The gate of Eden was later shut, and a flaming sword guarded the way to the tree of life. But remember the last page of the whole Bible: in Revelation 22 the tree of life appears again, growing inside the city on both sides of the river — and the gates of that city are never shut by day. The God who put the man in the garden brings the man home into the city at last.

The focus is not on how much I have accomplished, not on whether I have a family, and not on how tired I feel today. The focus is on Jesus — he is the God who bent down, and he is the Lord who breathed and said, "Receive the Holy Spirit." Not I, but Christ.
May God bless every one of us this week: to rest first and then work, to be placed first and then go out to cultivate and keep. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head, the second carries it from the head into the heart, the third carries it from the heart into the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at an idea.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear conviction.
1. ★ The first full day a human being ever lived was God's day of rest. What is that order saying? Say it in your own words; do not recite the manuscript.
2. ★★ The two verbs "cultivate and keep" are later used of a priest's service. How does that change the way you see your own work?
3. ★★★ God said, "It is not good for the man to be alone." What kind of "not good" does that mean in this chapter? Is it the same as what we usually call loneliness?
4. ★★ The human being of chapter 2 is dust plus the breath of God. If a person remembers only that he is dust, what does his life look like? And if he remembers only the breath?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, hearing, thinking, saying and walking, to digest the idea until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (things fall apart if I stop), fearful (I do not dare stop), ashamed (I do not deserve rest), wounded (nobody has ever carried anything for me). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "God blessed the seventh day, and made it holy." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ When did you last genuinely stop? What was holding you back at the time — the workload, or a sentence inside you? What was that sentence?
8. ★ Finish this in one sentence: "What have I been using to prove my worth?" If you are unsure, say instead what you are most afraid people think of you.
9. ★★ This week, in which stretch of time will you stop and hand sovereignty back to God? Name the day, the hour and how long.

Leader's reminder: questions eight and ten will touch exhaustion and guilt. If someone falls silent or weeps, stop the discussion and stay with him; do not rush to supply an answer, and never tell a person who is barely holding on that he "needs to rest more." If long-term burnout or depression is involved, follow up privately afterwards and help him find professional support.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ "Placed first, then put to work" — in your home this week, who most needs to be settled first? What will you do for that person?
11. ★ The same question in another setting: in your workplace or school, is there someone holding on alone?

12. ★★★ The ten-minute rest practice: each day this week pick a stretch of time in which you do nothing at all except hand over to God the one thing you can least put down. Say the time and the place.
13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — tell him your answer to question eleven this week, and ask him to check on you on the seventh day. Say his name now.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First, in the Bible the first full day a human being lived was the day of rest. Second, work existed before anyone had sinned, so work itself is good; what wears us out is the sense of futility. Third, so I have decided to keep ten minutes a day to stop and hand things over. Write down now who you will tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: the stretch of time you will stop this week, and who you will tell. Then pray for each other, asking the Lord that we would not hold this world up by our own strength, but enter and rest in the work he has already finished.
